speaker: Faye Dsouza
text: Tell me about Mrs. Deshpande because I saw a little bit of the teaser, the trailer. It's a very layered character. It is. speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: I think first of all, I love the fact that she's such a multi-layered character. it's She she can be very ordinary. I mean you you just look at her The ambiguity is there like she's just so she's just a housewife. She's so calm. She's composed. She's quiet She doesn't have to raise her voice, but she can make someone feel really uncomfortable you know just with the silences or with her calmness, you know and She can Just say something and just shake people up. And so I thought that that power that she has I I thought that was amazing, you know, and of course her whole history her her Backstory adds to whoever she is. Plus, like you said, a very complicated kind of relationship, which also plays on everybody's mind. And also the fact that even though she's working so closely with authorities, with the police, but it's not based on trust. It's just based on the fact that something heinous is happening. And we need to stop that. And that's why they need her help. But can you really trust her? She can be someone who can be spinning her own thing on the side saying that I'm out, but I have something else on my mind as well. So all these things, you know, that just adds to the mystery of her character. And I thought it would be wonderful to play her. And of course, Nagesh Kulkarnoor. is directing it and I have seen his past work and I've been an admirer. I loved Door, C.O.D., City of Dreams, his latest Hunt or Hyderabad Blues or Iqbal, all these films I had seen and I was very, very, I loved his work and then when he approached me as a director for this, I was like, yeah, I would love to do it. Because he's also a director who can extract that performance from you and keep the narrative and everything very precise, very concise, and not stray here and there. And applause, of course, was behind this whole project, who have done such good work before. And I said, yes, I would love to do this role. Also, it makes it I can do something different, you know, from what I've done so far. So it's not glamorous. She's not like, oh, beautiful and all that. She's like, she's someone who's very real, very, very raw, very off the earth, you know, and that's what I liked about her.

speaker: Faye Dsouza
text: You feel OTT now sort of creates more opportunities to write these characters of depth for women?

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: Absolutely. And that's how I've done Fame Game or Majama because it just gives me a chance to do something very different from what theatrical release will have. When you put a movie in a theater, you are bound by certain things that you think of. This is the audience. You have to please everyone in the audience. And so a lot of compromises are done to make a script palatable to everyone. But here, since there are no constraints of that kind, you can create stuff that is like just out of the box and and just just left of the field or you know the right of the field absolutely and That's why mrs. Deshpande was so important for me to do or a Majama or a fame game you know it gave me something so different to do so dramatic and and And also it gives you time to, you know, create your character and create that mystery and, you know, everything. So I think that's how it does. And, you know, also I think because of OTT, you also, you know, discover so much fresh talent as well. Right? How do you mean? In a sense, there's so much talent which doesn't have to look a particular way or be a particular way. They're talented people who have just come and just captured your imagination. Young people who have come with dreams in their eyes and they're here. They're doing such a good job, like they're acting so well. And so that kind of discovery has, the OTT has made it possible to do that. And tell like stories which are so diverse and the world's cinemized in front of you. You know, you get to see different cultures and you get to learn about so many different things. But I find that what finally boils down to is emotions. And that's the same everywhere. You know, we have the same issues, we have the same problem, but you see the same thing, but it's set in a different culture. That makes it very interesting.

speaker: Faye Dsouza
text: I thought it was interesting because in the blockbuster films that you did in the 90s, for example, there wasn't as much space for acting in the silences, which I know you've done here in Mr. Sesh Pandey, where a lot of the work is just with your face, but without saying anything. text: Because I did films which had a lot of silences too, like a prahar. See, for every Dil Toh Baagal Hai I did, there was a Mrityudan, you know. And that's the way I was brought up actually. Because my dad used to read the newspaper, see the reviews and then take us to watch films. So we have seen a lot of Shabana, Azmeer, those kind of films which were... art house films at that time. And we grew up on that. And when I started working in films, then when I was doing commercial films as well, there was always something very powerful. And I was very fortunate that I got to play those kind of roles, whether it's beta, Or a Raja where you know she's completely like dominating everything that's happening. Or Lajja Des Do Pagal Hai, or a Lajja, or a Mrityudand. You know so I got to do these different kind of roles which not only were commercial but also like Mrityudand had a lot of silences and there were a lot of things in that. So I think every commercial film there was something that I was doing which was commercial but yet it had those little nuances that you know.

text: What's the interesting challenge now with you know with the work that you're doing with television or with OTT?

speaker: Faye Dsouza
text: When you look back at your career, obviously successes and failures as everybody has had, what has been your secret in dealing with failure? speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: You know, every failure has made me angry in the sense It made me feel that, nah, I need to get out of this and I need to prove myself. So every failure I looked at, as like I tell my kids, as a learning curve, you know. And I always used to feel that when I've done a film, I've been on the set, I've done my best, you know, I've worked sincerely, I have given it all. Now I step back, the film releases, whether it does well or it doesn't do well, I have done my best. So I can rest assured that from my side there's been no cheating or nothing that, you know, I've given it my all. But if the film doesn't do well, then it's part of how films are. Some films work, some films don't work. But of course, sometimes it does hurt you. You do feel bad. But then it used to give me that rigor, that anger again, that saying that, nah, I'm going to prove myself. I'm going to do the next film, which is going to be even better. So that's how I looked at failure.

speaker: Faye Dsouza
text: Tell me what it was like when you decided to come back to your career from the US. I mean, I know everybody's asked you about your decision to leave, but your decision to come back because your husband had a thriving practice. He came back with you, you brought the kids back with you. Did you know what you were planning on doing with your career? Were you nervous? Saying, oh my God, is it going to work out?

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: See, every decision you make, of course, there's a little bit of nervousness in the sense that, oh, we're going to a new thing. But for me, I was just coming back home. So there was nothing to get nervous about. What motivated that? Well, there were a lot of things that happened. My parents were living with me and, you know, they wanted to come back because they were getting old. They wanted to be where, you know, they have grown up and, you know, it's comfortable here for them. My kids were growing up and you know, I was getting a lot of offers from here So I was coming here working going back and I was finding that very hard to you know continue doing because it it means a lot of time away from my kids and away from home and Ram was also like he wanted to do something different. He Here's a cardiothoracic surgeon and he had worked 20 years and you know, he said I I'm operating on people, you know, after the fact, you know, after everything is done and after they got sick, then they came to me and now I'm operating on them and getting them better. But what if I can get them before it happens? So there was something brewing in his mind, what he wanted to do, something that's different from what he was doing. And I want to come back. And everybody thought that my parents were the main deciding factor. And I said, OK, let's go back. Let's do this. Let's go back. So we had all the plans and everything before we made the move.

speaker: Faye Dsouza
text: When you're raising your children now, especially in the age of social media, It's perhaps a harsher time to be a teenager, to be a young person now than it has ever been before. Does that worry you? And that's not an India or a US thing that's currently just the way the world is. How do you navigate that as a parent?

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: Well, you know, sometimes you feel scared for your kids because Not everybody is that strong. Not everybody can have, you know, that resilience or that intelligence to know, you know, this is like, okay, you know, don't deal with this. This is what you got to deal with. And the navigation becomes a little difficult for them. But I think when you have given them the values, you know, like my, they grew up with my, my parents, so they grew up with their grandparents, they learned so much from them. We are trying to impart, you know, the best thing that we can do for them. giving them the values, respect everyone, you know, don't take things for granted, work hard for everything you do. And you know, we are giving them everything we can. And we're trying to raise kids who are strong, kids who can stand on their own feet. and kids who can stand up for themselves. So we are trying to do that. And we just hope that once they go into the world, they will use those tools that we have already placed in front of them, given them, and they will navigate life according to what we've taught them. But of course, there will be ups and downs in everybody's lives, and how you deal with that becomes the crux of everything.

speaker: Faye Dsouza

text: Well, I would say the same thing that my mom told me. You know, you have to be comfortable in your own skin. This is who you are. And you don't... How do I put it? What you do with your life, how you lead your life, you know, stay healthy, that's the most important thing. Do good things, work hard. You just concentrate on those aspects of your life that makes you who you are.

I'm going to keep in that because it just makes me feel good. It's very spiritual for me. It also adds a lot to who you are.

He said that's it. So I said, okay, let's go shopping now.

So for me, being married, having kids and having a house, that was a part of my dream. So when I was doing that, I was living a dream. And of course, work is also a very important part of your life because that's your own personal selfish thing that you want to do. Not selfish, but I would say that it's something that you do. You feed your soul. Yes, you feed your soul. So I felt that I missed my craft, but I loved every minute of those five years that I was away too.

speaker: Faye Dsouza
text: I think it's very interesting for me because I feel that our generation of women, unlike our mothers, who some of them did work, but it wasn't such a large part of their identity. You learn from your parents. And that's what I learned from her, that how she managed everything and yet did something that she loved.

By the time 15-20 years went away from the end of the war, so you're in the early 60s, It became pretty clear that Europe and Japan were back into a rebuilding and growth phase and attention began to focus into the rest of the world in the so-called emerging world at that time and more parts of the bank got created one called the International Development Association, IDA, which caters for what is the poorest countries on the planet. Today, 78 countries are in that category. And essentially, the difference between that and the IBRD is that those countries get one third, roughly, of the money we give. It's free. No repayment of interest or principle. Whereas IBRD is closer to commercial market terms, but the concessionality of IBRD comes from the fact that you give long-term loans longer than what you could get from a bank or from markets in your country. The third thing that got created was the International Finance Corporation. That goes to the private sector and enables the private sector to invest by de-risking in emerging market stuff. India is a classic example of that. Most people don't know, but HDFC, originally started with an IFC investment. And today is your largest private bank and has got an enormous footprint both in mortgages and helped to create the mortgage market in some ways in India, but also did a great job in the private banking side of financial services. The head of the judge, the head of the bench will say, for instance, if I was the Chief Justice, I would say, sisters and brothers, I'll write the first cut on this and then I'll circulate my judgment to you.
